description.description: Object description (e.g., 'wooden barrel', 'stone fountain')

width.description: Canvas width in pixels (required for basic mode, auto-detected from background_image if provided)

height.description: Canvas height in pixels (required for basic mode, auto-detected from background_image if provided)

view.description: Camera angle

background_image.description: Background image for style matching (optional). Format: {"type": "base64", "base64": "..."}. File paths are not supported (server cannot read local files). If provided without inpainting config, uses default: oval 60%.

inpainting.description: Inpainting configuration as JSON string (optional). DEFAULT: If background_image provided but this omitted, uses oval 0.6. Options: {"type": "oval", "fraction": 0.3} for auto oval mask, {"type": "rectangle", "fraction": 0.5} for auto rectangle mask, {"type": "mask", "mask_image": "base64..."} for custom mask. Mask convention: WHITE (255) = area where AI generates, BLACK (0) = frozen/preserved context. Fraction is 0.05-0.95 (how much of background the shape covers).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_music
tools.description:
Make music for your game: two takes of a song from a description of its style.

Instrumental by default; with vocals, send lyrics or set auto_lyrics. Both takes
are saved to your library on the website, where they can go in your games.
restyle_song_id plays one of your songs again in a new style. For music that
repeats seamlessly, call make_music_loop on a finished instrumental take.

Cost: 10 generations, or $0.08 in credits, for the two takes; charged once they
are made. Needs a tier 2 subscription or higher.

Generation time: ~20-60 seconds, up to 2.5 minutes when busy (async). Poll with
get_music or wait_for_jobs; the result is an audio link (MP3).

Example: create_music(style="Upbeat 8-bit dungeon theme: a fast square-wave lead,
a pulsing triangle bass and crisp noise drums, ending on a sting.", bpm=140)

schema.name: mcp__pixellab__create_music
schema.description:
Make music for your game: two takes of a song from a description of its style.

Instrumental by default; with vocals, send lyrics or set auto_lyrics. Both takes
are saved to your library on the website, where they can go in your games.
restyle_song_id plays one of your songs again in a new style. For music that
repeats seamlessly, call make_music_loop on a finished instrumental take.

Cost: 10 generations, or $0.08 in credits, for the two takes; charged once they
are made. Needs a tier 2 subscription or higher.

Generation time: ~20-60 seconds, up to 2.5 minutes when busy (async). Poll with
get_music or wait_for_jobs; the result is an audio link (MP3).

Example: create_music(style="Upbeat 8-bit dungeon theme: a fast square-wave lead,
a pulsing triangle bass and crisp noise drums, ending on a sting.", bpm=140)

style.description: What the music sounds like, in a sentence or two that gives each instrument a role, plus the mood and how it ends: 'Calm chiptune town theme: a soft square-wave melody over a bouncy bass, light noise drums, ending on a held chord.' A list of tags comes out flat; artist names are refused. Put sounds to keep out in exclude, not as 'no ...' here. improve_music_style writes a short idea out in full.

instrumental.description: true: no vocals (game music). false: a song with vocals, which needs lyrics or auto_lyrics.

lyrics.description: With vocals: the words to sing, one line per line, with section tags on their own lines: [Intro], [Verse], [Pre-Chorus], [Chorus], [Bridge], [Instrumental Break], [Outro], [End]. A tag can carry one direction: [Chorus: full band, doubled vocals]. write_music_lyrics drafts some.

auto_lyrics.description: With vocals: have the lyrics written for the song instead of sending them (send no lyrics, length_s or style_weight). get_music shows what it sings once it is made.

about.description: With auto_lyrics: what the song is about; may be empty.

length_s.description: Length to aim for, 10-360 s. Default: auto, fitted to the song (a new style: the song's own length).

bpm.description: Tempo, 60-180 BPM, added to the style. Default: auto.

voice.description: With vocals: the voice, added to the style, e.g. 'warm female voice', 'bright female voice', 'breathy female voice', 'powerful female voice'. Ignored for instrumentals.

exclude.description: Sounds to keep out, short phrases: 'fade out, electric guitar'. An instrumental keeps out 'vocals, singing' without being asked.

style_weight.description: How closely to follow the style, 0-1. Default: 0.5.

name.description: The song's name in the library. Default: the style's first words. The second take gets ' (take 2)'.

restyle_song_id.description: Make one of your songs again in this new style: the same melody, its vocals and lyrics kept (send no lyrics, auto_lyrics or about).

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished song is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_normal_map
tools.description:
Make the normal map of a sprite or an animation, so a game engine can light it
(Pro 0.5 generation, Lite 0.1 generation).

The map is a PNG the sprite's size: RGB = which way each pixel faces (red right,
green up in the opengl convention, blue toward the viewer), alpha 255 wherever the
sprite shows and 0 elsewhere.
Each part of the sprite gets its own shape — a head is round, a hat a cone, a wall
faces south — so a light moving around it shades it the way a 3D model would.

An animation (`character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>`, a GIF, a strip) comes
back as a strip, one map per frame side by side in frame order, made from one
plan so the light stays steady as it moves.

Use it in Phaser with the Light2D pipeline:
  this.load.image('knight', ['knight.png', 'knight_n.png'])
  sprite.setPipeline('Light2D'); this.lights.enable().setAmbientColor(0x555555)
Godot: assign it as the sprite's normal map (CanvasTexture). Unreal: convention
"directx".

Each slider left out starts where the kind of picture puts it (an isometric box
gets flat faces), which suits most pictures. Lower
surface_detail for clean flat-shaded art, raise part_shapes for a rounder body;
strength makes the whole map stronger or flatter. Cracks, holes and gaps between
plates come out as grooves even when they glow.

mode="lite" (the default, recommended) reads the map from the art alone in about a
second and is almost always as good; mode="pro" plans every part (a head, an arm in
front of the body, a crack sunk in).

Any colours work (painted art too); pixel art gives the cleanest parts.
Cost: Pro 0.5 generation, Lite 0.1 generation — per CALL, not per frame, so a
32-frame strip maps for the same 0.1 as a single sprite and is by far the
cheapest way to light an animation. Charged only when the map is delivered.
One call takes up to 32 frames at 8-512 px a side; a longer animation has to
be split, which costs one charge per call and plans each part separately, so
the lighting can step between them. Time: Pro ~15-60 s, Lite a few seconds
(async). Poll with get_image(job_id).

image.description: The sprite: `character:<id>:<direction>` (a rotation), `character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>` (every frame of that animation), the same for `object:<id>`, `gallery:<id>`, `job:<id>` (an image tool result), `upload:<id>`, a pixelart_workbench result id, an https or data URL of a PNG or GIF, or base64. Prefer a reference or URL to inline base64.

convention.description: opengl: green = up (Godot, Unity, Phaser, most engines); directx: green = down (Unreal).

mode.description: lite (0.1 generation, recommended): from the art alone, in about a second, and almost always as good; set kind with it for isometric, sidescroller and UI art. pro (0.5 generation): each part of the picture is planned, its shape, what is in front, what is sunk into it.

kind.description: What the picture is: character (a character, creature or portrait), object (an item or effect), topdown (a map, scene or tileset seen from above), side (a side view: sidescroller tiles, a landscape), iso (isometric tiles and objects) or ui (panels, buttons, frames). Left out, it is read from the picture; set it when you know, above all for sidescroller, isometric and UI art.

strength.description: How far every pixel tilts away from facing the viewer.

outline_rounding.description: How much the outline rounds off: 0 keeps it flat to the edge.

part_shapes.description: How much the sprite's 3D parts (a round head, an arm's cylinder) add.

surface_detail.description: The art's own light and dark as bumps: chunks bulge, dark lines and cracks sink.

detail_softness.description: How much that detail is blurred, in px: low follows every pixel.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_object_pro_flash
tools.description:
Create a Pro Flash object from text, with one direction or eight V3 views.

Supply description, optional width/height (default 64x64), and style_image.
For props that match a game's characters, pass the same anchor sprite as

description says. For a profile or other facing with n_directions=1, make
it with create_image_pro_flash and pass its id as source_image_id.

download its PNG (one direction) or ZIP (eight). No preview is regenerated.

to 96px, 6 from 100 to 208, 9 from 212 to 256 — so 32x96 and 64x48 are both
5. n_directions=8 adds a rotation charge, billed separately, and the
TOTAL by longest side is the same ladder the character tool uses:
6 for 16-88; 7 for 92-96; 8 for 100-128; 9 for 132-156; 10 for 160-180; 11 for 184-200; 12 for 204-208; 15 for 212-220; 16 for 224-236; 17 for 240-256. The steps are uneven, so read the band rather than interpolating;
get_pro_flash_capabilities(operation="object", width=, height=,
n_directions=) quotes the split for free. Reusing a first frame bills only the rotation
part, and nothing at all for one direction.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_object_state
tools.description:
Queue a state (variant) of an existing object. Auto-waits up to 30s for the
source object to complete. Returns a new object ID grouped with the source
via group_id.

An object is a group of states: `name` is the object's name (shared by all
states), and each state has its own `state_name` — defaulting to the edit
description truncated to 20 characters (a new object's first state is named
"base"). Pass `state_name` to name the new state explicitly.

A state is the SAME object in another condition (open/closed, lit, broken).
A different item belongs in its own object — for a matching look, pass the
source's image as style_images to create_1_direction_object. States move
together: adding or removing one in a project or folder moves every state.

`palette` (hex colours, plus `palette_name`) puts the state, every direction of
it, on those colours; the source goes on them before the edit.

Cost: known before the call, and the receipt repeats it. It is ONE charge for
the whole state, covering every direction the source has — there is no
per-direction price. An 8-direction state edited from text goes by the
frame's LONGEST side — 10 generations up
to 84px, 15 from 85 to 112, 25 above. Every other state (a 1-direction
object, or any state given a reference image) is priced like the other
canvas tools: 10 up to a square 256x256, 15 to 341x341, 25 above, measured
at the frame's own aspect ratio rather than its longest side.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_path_tiles
tools.description:
Create a connectable PATH/ROAD tile set (18 configs).

Generates straights, corners, T-junctions, a crossroads, dead-ends and a
plain ground tile, all sharing one look. The set ships per-tile edge rules
(N/E/S/W bitmasks), so a map editor or your own autotiler can pick the right
piece from a cell's painted neighbours — see get_tiles_pro for the rules.

For terrain transitions (grass meeting water) use
create_tiles_pro(tile_feature="tileset"); for walls and floors use
create_building_kit.

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec)
pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: the set is drawn for them
and every pixel of every tile is one of them.

Cost: 10-25 generations, set by the SHEET its road set is drawn on — and that
set is never shrunk to reach a cheaper canvas the way create_tiles_pro's
independent tiles are, so tile_view_angle moves the price as much as tile_size.
A square_topdown set only takes tile_size=32, where the default angle prices it
at 15, tile_view_angle=90 (straight down, so the cells are at their tallest) at
25, and a near-side angle at 10. isometric takes 48-96: 48px is 10 at any
angle, 64px is 10 (15 at 90), and 96px is 25 unless the angle is near-side.
Flatter art is the cheaper art here.

Non-blocking: returns a tile id immediately; poll with get_tiles_pro.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_portrait_character
tools.description:
Convert between a portrait and a character sprite (pro).

Preserves the subject's identity/outfit while matching an internal
size-specific pixel-art style for the chosen view. For a fixed palette
(Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours:
the sprite is drawn for them and every pixel is one of them.

This tool starts asynchronous generation that returns immediately with a job
ID. Use get_portrait_character to check status and retrieve the sprite.

Examples:
- Turn a character portrait into a top-down RPG sprite:
  create_portrait_character(image_url=<portrait_png_url>, direction="portrait_to_character", view="low top-down", result_size=64)
- Turn a full-body sprite into a bust portrait:
  create_portrait_character(image_url=<character_png_url>, direction="character_to_portrait", view="low top-down", result_size=64)

Generation time: ~30-80 seconds (async processing)

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_room
tools.description:
Paint one room (a 7 x 6 grid of 32 px floor cells; top-down 256x256 px, or isometric) as pixel
art, built and furnished for its theme (a castle's, a house's, a starship's), its doorways
where `doors` puts them so rooms join up on a map; the rock round its walls is transparent.
A top-down room's building kit can also come as a 16, 24, 48 or 64 px tileset (tile_size).
Takes ~4 minutes (1 in 10 over 8); returns a room id at once.
Costs 20 generations when the room is ready (25 with tile_size 48 or 64; 10 more for its
pieces). Needs Tier 1 (Pixel Apprentice) or higher.

schema.name: mcp__pixellab__create_room
schema.description:
Paint one room (a 7 x 6 grid of 32 px floor cells; top-down 256x256 px, or isometric) as pixel
art, built and furnished for its theme (a castle's, a house's, a starship's), its doorways
where `doors` puts them so rooms join up on a map; the rock round its walls is transparent.
A top-down room's building kit can also come as a 16, 24, 48 or 64 px tileset (tile_size).
Takes ~4 minutes (1 in 10 over 8); returns a room id at once.
Costs 20 generations when the room is ready (25 with tile_size 48 or 64; 10 more for its
pieces). Needs Tier 1 (Pixel Apprentice) or higher.

theme.description: What the room is, in one line: what it is and where decide its walls, floor and furniture (e.g. "The bridge of a starship.", "A blacksmith's forge under a castle.")

doors.description: The doors, 1-8 of {"side": "n"|"e"|"s"|"w", "col": 0-6, "row": 0-5}: n = a door in a back wall (the wall above a floor cell), e/w = an open doorway in the right/left wall beside a cell (two cells tall: `row` is the upper one), s = an open doorway in the bottom wall below a cell. Each must sit on a wall of the floor, and an e/w doorway needs two cells of wall between it and an inner corner below it. Example for the full room: [{"side": "s", "col": 3, "row": 5}, {"side": "w", "col": 0, "row": 2}]

cells.description: The floor plan, seen from above: 6 rows of 7 characters, '#' floor and '.' solid rock, the floor in one piece. Left out: the whole 7 x 6 grid is floor. An L-shaped room: ["####...", "####...", "#######", "#######", "#######", "#######"]

name.description: Optional name; named from the theme when left out.

pieces.description: Also cut the furniture out as movable pieces, each with its own shadow, to move, remove or reuse in the website's room editor (~5-8 more minutes, charged on its own). Only when the user wants to rearrange the furniture: the painted room is complete without it, and cut_out_room_furniture does it later.

style_room_id.description: A style room: another of the user's finished rooms (its room_id) whose look the new room takes (the same walls, wall tops, floor, door, wall lights and hanging), so rooms of one building join up. The shape (cells, doors) and the furniture are the new room's own; `theme` then says what this room is ("its kitchen"). It must be in the same view as the new room.

style_room_floor.description: With style_room_id: take the style room's floor too. False gives the new room its own floor, decided by `theme` ("its chapel, with a wooden floor"), under the style room's walls, wall tops, door, wall lights and hanging.

view.description: top-down: the back walls' faces show above the floor (256x256 px). isometric: 2:1 isometric, the n and w walls tall with their doors in them, the s and e walls low curbs with open doorways; the same cells and doors, a picture of about 248x176 px for the full grid. oblique: the floor a square grid seen from above, heights leaning up and to the left, the n and w walls tall, the s and e walls low curbs; walls, doors and floor only, no furniture yet (pieces must be false); about 272x240 px for the full grid.

project_id.description: A project of yours to file the room in (list_projects); a game also uses it, so a Game Builder workspace gets it under assets/rooms/{room_id}/. Left out: your auto-add setting.

tile_size.description: Top-down rooms only: the tile size of the tileset its building kit comes as. 32 is the room's own; 16, 24, 48 or 64 also paints the kit at that size, so the kit download (get_room's `building kit (zip)`) holds a tileset-15 sheet and its metadata at that size too. The room's picture stays 32 px cells. 48 or 64 costs 25 generations instead of 20.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_sidescroller_tileset
tools.description:
Generate a sidescroller tileset for 2D platformer games with side-view perspective.

This tool starts an asynchronous tileset generation that returns immediately with a tileset ID.
Use get_sidescroller_tileset to check status and retrieve the completed tileset.

Which mode: standard (default) is the website's standard sidescroller tileset
(pixen, side view), cheap and fast. mode="pro" paints the richest platforms;
use it when the look matters, standard when cost does.

Cost: standard is 1 generation now that it runs on pixen. (The classic model
it replaced billed 2 or 3 generations — NOT 1, over 1,186 prod charges, mean
2.6.) mode="pro" costs 15 generations for tiles up to 32 px and 25 above
that — the same ladder top-down pro uses, since both read one price(). Failed jobs are
not charged.

Creates tilesets optimized for 2D platformer games:
- Side-view perspective (not top-down)
- Transparent background (no background terrain)
- Platform/ground tiles with flat surfaces (no slopes)
- Optional decorative transition layer on top of base terrain

Use case: Building 2D platformer games with seamless terrain tiles.

## Creating Connected Tilesets

Use base tile IDs to create multiple tilesets that seamlessly connect:

1. Create first tileset (e.g., stone platform, either mode) and wait for completion
2. Use get_sidescroller_tileset to retrieve the base tile ID
3. Pass that base tile ID with mode="pro" to create the next tileset

Chaining needs mode="pro": standard draws the new top around every edge of a
chained platform instead of only on top.

The base tile is the platform body: chaining reuses it and draws a new top.
Example workflow:
- Tileset 1: stone brick platform, grass on top → get base tile ID
- Tileset 2: stone brick platform, snow on top (stone base tile ID, mode="pro")
- Tileset 3: stone brick platform, moss on top (same base tile ID, mode="pro")

A different body (wood, metal) is a new tileset without base_tile_id.

platform_thickness (standard only) sets how thick the platforms are, as the
website's Platform Thickness slider; omitted, it adapts to transition_size.

Generation time: standard ~30 seconds, pro a few minutes (async processing)

transition_size.description: Size of terrain transition. Controls how much of the surface layer appears (0.0 = no surface layer, 0.25 = light surface layer, 0.5 = heavy surface layer). Snapped to the nearest of 0, 0.25 and 0.5.

mode.description: Pro needs a Tier 1+ plan (not a trial). "standard": the website's standard sidescroller tileset (pixen, side view), cheap and fast. "pro": the richest platforms - painted texture, a cleaner cap - use it when the look matters.

enhance.description: mode='standard' only. AI-enhances the platform and surface descriptions and picks matching base colours before generation. The stored tileset keeps the enhanced text; your original prompts are kept in its metadata.

platform_thickness.description: mode='standard' only. How thick the platform body is, 0 = thin to 1 = thick; omit to adapt it to transition_size (the website's 'auto').

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_sound_effect
tools.description:
Make a sound effect for your game from a description: hits, shots, explosions,
footsteps, creatures, UI clicks, ambience.

One clip per call (WAV); call again for another take. It is saved to your
library on the website, where it can go in your games.

Cost: by length, charged once the clip is made: 1 generation up to 1.6 s, 2 up
to 3.2 s, 4 at 6 s, 7 at 10 s, 19 at 30 s (0.614 per second, rounded up); in
credits $0.0027 per second. Needs a tier 2 subscription or higher.

Generation time: ~5-20 seconds (async). Poll with get_sound_effect or
wait_for_jobs.

Example: create_sound_effect(prompt="a sci-fi laser gun firing a single shot",
seconds=1)

Make a sound effect for your game from a description: hits, shots, explosions,
footsteps, creatures, UI clicks, ambience.

One clip per call (WAV); call again for another take. It is saved to your
library on the website, where it can go in your games.

Cost: by length, charged once the clip is made: 1 generation up to 1.6 s, 2 up
to 3.2 s, 4 at 6 s, 7 at 10 s, 19 at 30 s (0.614 per second, rounded up); in
credits $0.0027 per second. Needs a tier 2 subscription or higher.

Generation time: ~5-20 seconds (async). Poll with get_sound_effect or
wait_for_jobs.

Example: create_sound_effect(prompt="a sci-fi laser gun firing a single shot",
seconds=1)

prompt.description: The sound in plain words: 'a heavy sword slash hitting metal armor', 'footsteps walking on gravel at a steady pace', 'steady rain on a roof with distant thunder'.

seconds.description: Clip length, 0.5-30 s (to 0.1 s). A shot or hit: ~1 s; an explosion or growl: ~3 s; an ambience: 10-30 s.

name.description: The clip's name in the library. Default: the prompt's first words.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished clip is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_talking_gif
tools.description:
Turn text into a talking GIF using a character's existing mouth positions.

FREE — no generations are spent. This only sequences frames that
create_vocal_animation already produced, so the expensive step happens once
per expression and every line of dialogue after that costs nothing.

Examples:
- create_talking_gif(character_id="<uuid>", text_to_speak="Welcome, traveller!")
- create_talking_gif(character_id="<uuid>", text_to_speak="You dare return?!", mood="angry")
- portrait-only, no character:
  create_talking_gif(from_job_id="<vocal job id>", text_to_speak="Hello!")

Returns immediately (no job to poll).

character_id.description: Character with a vocal animation. Mutually exclusive with `from_job_id`.

from_job_id.description: Use a portrait-only set instead: the job id from create_vocal_animation(image=...). Mutually exclusive with `character_id`. Available for 8 hours after that job finished.

hold_ms.description: Pause on the closed mouth at the end so a looping GIF has a beat between takes.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_tiles_pro
tools.description:
Create pixel art tiles (pro): up to 16 independent tiles of one shape per
call. Returns a tile id at once; poll get_tiles_pro(tile_id) (~1-2 min).
Needs a tier 1 subscription or higher.

- Shape mode (default): tile_type, tile_size, tile_view; number each tile.
- Style mode: style_images sets style and size; shape controls are ignored.
- tile_feature="tileset": a connectable terrain transition ("grass to water"),
  16 corner tiles or a 32-tile hex coastline; oblique exists only as this.
- palette + palette_name: every pixel is one of your hex colours.

Other tools: square top-down terrain transitions -> create_topdown_tileset
(transition width, per-terrain references, style matching); paths ->
create_path_tiles; walls, floors and oblique buildings -> create_building_kit.

Cost: priced by the sheet, 16 cells of the tile AS DRAWN, so tile_view,
tile_view_angle, tile_depth_ratio and tile_height move it as well as tile_size.
Independent tiles: 10 generations while that sheet stays small, else 15; they
never reach 25 (for every type but oblique: 16-48px 10, 64px 10 or 15 by view,
larger mostly 15; oblique extrudes side faces, 15 from 64px). Tilesets reach
15 or 25 at 96px and above. The sheet holds 16 tiles up to 64px for every type
but oblique; above that take get_tiles_pro's count rather than planning on 16.

Full reference (cost by size and view, map rules, every parameter):
search_help(tool="create_tiles_pro").

description.description: Number each tile: '1). grass tile 2). stone tile 3). lava tile'. At most 16 independent tiles per call: split a longer list. A tileset: the transition, e.g. 'grass to water'.

tile_type.description: hex flat-top, hex_pointy pointy-top, isometric diamond, octagon, square_topdown square at an angle. oblique (square top, depth extruded down-right) needs tile_feature='tileset'.

tile_size.description: Tile size in px; 32 is recommended.

tile_height.description: Non-square tiles, e.g. 128 for 64x128. Maps take groups made without tile_height (or with tile_size or 2x it): for a flat 2:1 iso floor omit it and set tile_view_angle=30 and tile_depth_ratio=0.

tile_view_angle.description: Degrees, overrides tile_view: 0 side, 90 top-down; isometric 30 is 2:1.

tile_flat_top_px.description: Isometric only: top/bottom cap width, 2 classic or 4 modern.

style_images.description: Tiles to copy style and size from; shape controls are then ignored. Each {"image": "<reference>"} (URL, upload:, gallery:, job: or pixel tool id) or inline {"base64", "width", "height"}.

style_options.description: What to copy from style_images, as JSON: {"color_palette": true, "outline": true, "detail": true, "shading": true}

outline_mode.description: "outline": grey shading with outlines. "segmentation": red/blue zones, no outlines, cleaner tiles.

tile_feature.description: "tileset": a connectable terrain transition instead of independent tiles (the first terrain is the main one), with placement rules. Not with style_images.

oblique_lean.description: Oblique tilesets: shear per pixel of depth, 0.5 cabinet, 1 = 45 degrees (default).

boundary_amplitude.description: tile_feature='tileset' only (square_topdown, isometric, oblique, hex, hex_pointy). Uneven boundary: how far the terrain border meanders instead of a straight edge, 0 = straight (default) to 0.3. Tiles still connect seamlessly.

boundary_seed.description: Boundary shape for boundary_amplitude (the website's Reshuffle): another number gives a different coastline at the same amount.

elevation.description: tile_feature='tileset' on square_topdown, isometric or oblique only. Terrain height in pixels: raises the first terrain into a plateau with a cliff face down to the second. 0 = flat (default), at most 12; the cap is what fits the tile's top face and wall at this size and view, and a larger value is refused with it.

step_slope.description: Edge steepness, with elevation above 0: how far the drop spreads sideways. 0 = a cliff straight down (default), up to 2 = a gentle slope over more ground (the website steps it by 0.25).

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_topdown_tileset
tools.description:
Generate a Wang tileset (corner-based autotiling) joining two terrains for a
top-down map. Returns a tileset id at once; poll get_topdown_tileset (standard
~30 s, pro a few minutes).

Modes: standard (default) is the website's standard tileset, cheap and fast,
16/24/32 px tiles. mode="pro" paints the richest tiles (textured ground, raised
banks, more shape controls), 16/32/64 px, Tier 1+: use it when the look
matters. transition_size sets the bank/wall height; a tall set has 25 tiles.

One tileset holds exactly two terrains; three or more need a chain: pass the
shared terrain's base tile id from get_topdown_tileset as the next set's
lower_base_tile_id/upper_base_tile_id. Standard redraws that terrain close, not
byte-identical; pro pastes it exactly. mode="pro" takes palette (plus
palette_name) or max_colors; standard takes neither.

Standard sometimes swaps the two terrains, far more often with grass as lower:
on a flat set put grass upper, and check each sheet's all-lower tile.

Cost: standard is 1 generation; mode="pro" costs 15 generations for tiles up
to 32 px, 25 above. Failed jobs are not charged.

Full reference (tile counts, shape controls, chaining, terrain order):
search_help(tool="create_topdown_tileset").

transition_description.description: The strip between the terrains, e.g. 'wet sand with foam'; used only when transition_size > 0.

tile_size.description: Square: {"width": N, "height": N} or a bare int N. 16, 24 or 32 for standard; 16, 32 or 64 for mode='pro'.

mode.description: "standard": cheap and fast. "pro": the richest painted tiles, needs a Tier 1+ plan (not a trial). See the tool description.

enhance.description: Standard only: AI-enhances the terrain descriptions before drawing; your own prompts are kept in metadata.

spread_x.description: No effect; kept so existing calls work.

slope_size.description: No effect; kept so existing calls work.

raggedness.description: Terrain boundary wobble, 0 = clean lines to 1 = rough. Both modes; tall pro sets (transition_size above 0.4) are half as rough. Omit for the generator's default: 0 on pro, 0.45 on standard (the website's Standard tab starts at 0).

shape_seed.description: mode='standard'. Which wobble raggedness draws (0-99, the website's Reshuffle): another number gives a different boundary at the same raggedness.

boundary_seed.description: Which meander boundary_amplitude draws; another number, another shape.

step_slope.description: Pro with transition_size 0.25 only: the bank from a cliff (0) to a gentle slope.

outline.description: No effect; kept so existing calls work.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_ui_asset
tools.description:
Queue a pixel-art UI panel (10-25 generations, ~2-4 min). Returns ui_asset_id immediately.
Omit `pieces` for a default rounded-rect panel. Use get_ui_asset to check status.
For a fixed palette (Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as
its hex colours: the panel is drawn for them and every pixel is one of them.

Cost: 10 generations for a canvas up to 256x256, 15 up to 341x341, 25 above
— so the 256x256 default is the cheap option and 512x512 is 25. A non-square
panel is measured at its own aspect ratio, which is more generous than its
longer side: a 16:9 panel is 10 up to 341x192, 15 to 456x256, 25 from 457
wide. There is no quote endpoint; the response reports the actual charge.

Make states for UI elements (split from a template with update_ui_asset(split=True)): hover,
pressed, disabled, selected, or anything you describe. Each becomes a UI asset
of kind state under its element, in the same art. Returns a job id at once

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_vocal_animation
tools.description:
Generate a talking mouth-position set ("visemes") for a character's portrait.

Produces one keyframe per mouth shape, all sharing the chosen expression, so
the character can be lip-synced to any line of text afterwards. Building the
set costs generations ONCE; turning it into talking animations with
create_talking_gif is free.

Works two ways. With `character_id` the set is saved onto that character, so
every later call needs only the id — use this when the character exists.
With `image` you generate straight from a portrait and nothing is stored; the
frames live in the job for 8 hours and you reference it by job id.

Cost: 3 generations for the default 7 mouth positions on a portrait up to
64px. Two things scale it — the position count sets how many drawing passes
run (2 passes for 3 positions, 3 for 5 or 7, 4 for 12) and the portrait's size
sets what one pass costs (1 generation up to 64px, 2 at 96-128px, 4 at 160px,
5 at 192px, 8 at 256px). So 7 positions is 3 at 64px, 6 at 128px and 24 at
256px, while 12 positions on a 64px portrait is 4. engine="pixminimax" prices
a pass at 1 generation at every size, so a big portrait is far cheaper there.
A set can need a few extra passes to fill in a position, so the figure in the
submit receipt is the one to quote; those extra passes stop once a call
reaches 40 generations, which is the ceiling for any size and count. Turning
the set into talking animations with create_talking_gif is free, however many
lines you lip-sync.

Requires a subscription (or trial). The character form needs a portrait set
first. To delete an expression again:
set_character_portrait(character_id, remove_expression="angry").

Examples:
- Default talking set for a character:
  create_vocal_animation(character_id="<uuid>")
- Add an angry expression to the same character:
  create_vocal_animation(character_id="<uuid>", mood="angry")
- Just a portrait, no character:
  create_vocal_animation(image=<portrait_png>)

Generation time: ~2-5 minutes (async processing)

  create_vocal_animation(character_id="<uuid>")
- Add an angry expression to the same character:
  create_vocal_animation(character_id="<uuid>", mood="angry")
- Just a portrait, no character:

image.description: Generate from this portrait PNG (base64) instead, without a character. viseme_count.description: How many mouth positions to generate. 3 = minimal (tiny portraits), 5 = basic, 7 = recommended, 12 = high quality (large close-ups). Must match across moods for the same character.

no_background.description: Cut out the background so frames are transparent PNGs — usually what you want for compositing over a game scene.

engine.description: Which generator draws the mouth positions. 'v3' (default) is the original one. tools.name: mcp__pixellab__edit_animation
tools.description:
Edit an animation with a text instruction (pro): the same change on every
frame, each frame's pose and the motion kept.

edit_animation(frames=["character:<id>:east:<group id>"], description="add a
red cape")

Which edit tool:
- one image, or the same edit on separate images (a character's directions):
  edit_image (edit_image_pixen for a cheap single sprite)
- an animation's frames, changed by a text instruction: edit_animation (this)
- an animation's frames, re-dressed from a reference image: transfer_outfit

Needs 2+ frames. Frame limit by output size (the larger side): up to 64px 16
frames, up to 80px 9, up to 256px 4 — split a longer animation across calls
with the same description and seed. The result is NOT written back to a stored
character; save_to_asset does that (same frame count and size).

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from
Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: every pixel of
every frame is one of them.

Needs a tier 1 subscription or higher.
Cost: by the whole grid, not the frame count — 2 frames cost the same as 16
at 64x64, so batch them. One ascending ladder by FRAME size, both sides
counting: 16-128 px: 10 | 129-170: 15 | 171-256: 25. So 64x64, 80x80 and
128x128 are all 10 while 160x160 is 15 and 200x200 is 25 — these are NOT
edit_image's bands (that tool stays 10 all the way to 256x256), because
frames above 128px still sit on a 2x2 sheet here. Frames per call: 16 up to
64px, 9 up to 80, 4 above. ~2 minutes (async). Poll
get_image(job_id); frames come back in input order.

frames.description: The animation, in order. One entry for a whole animation: `character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>` or `object:<id>:<direction>:<animation>` (the [group: ...] id or name get_character / get_object shows), `job:<id>` (an animate_image / edit_image result), a GIF URL, or a multi-frame pixelart_workbench result. Or one entry per frame: https/data URLs, `upload:<id>`, `job:<id>:<index>` or base64 PNGs. Every frame the same size, max 256x256.

description.description: The edit to make on every frame: 'add a red cape', 'make the sword glow blue', 'give him a helmet'. Poses and motion stay as they are.

width.description: Output frame width. Defaults to the frames' width. Larger than the frames pads them with transparency, centred — never scales.

height.description: Output frame height. Defaults to the frames' height.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__edit_image
tools.description:
Edit an existing image with a text instruction or a reference image (pro).

This returns YOUR image, edited — the pose, composition and pixel style are
preserved and only what you asked for changes. Use it to recolour armour, add
an accessory, change an expression, or restyle frames to match a reference.

Two modes, picked by what you pass:
- text edit: edit_image(images_base64=[<png>], description="give him a red cape")
- reference edit: edit_image(images_base64=[<png>], reference_image_base64=<png>)

Which edit tool:
- one image, or the same edit on separate images (a character's directions):
  edit_image (this; edit_image_pixen is cheaper for a single sprite)
- an animation's frames, changed by a text instruction: edit_animation
- an animation's frames, re-dressed from a reference image: transfer_outfit
Reference mode here is for one image.

Related tools: create_image_pixflux(init_image_base64=...) regenerates the whole image
instead of editing it; create_map_object generates a NEW object matching a
map's style and returns a cutout, not your edited image.

Frame limit depends on output size: <=64px 16 frames, <=80px 9, <=128px 4,
larger 1 (one fewer in reference mode). Inputs max 512x512.

Cost: 10 generations for any output canvas up to 256x256, 15 up to 341x341,
25 above — so 64x64, 128x128 and 256x256 all cost the same 10, and the frame
grid is already priced in: a single 64x64 edit costs the same as sixteen of
them, so batch your frames where they fit. A non-square canvas is measured at
its own aspect ratio and can land a band lower than its longer side suggests.
HOW MANY frames fit is a separate ladder from the price and shares none of
its steps: 16 frames up to 64px, 9 up to 80px, 4 up to 128px, and a single
frame at any larger size (one fewer in reference mode, where the reference
takes a cell). So sixteen 64x64 frames are one call at 10, while 263 icons at
144x144 are 263 calls at 10 each — batching pays only up to 128px, and above
it the price per call is unchanged.
Generation time: ~30-90 seconds (async). Poll with get_image(job_id).

images_base64.description: Base64 PNG(s) to edit — pass a one-element list for a single image. Several frames get the SAME edit applied consistently (useful for animation frames or a character's directions). Max 512x512 each. PREFER image_urls — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

description.description: What to change (e.g. 'add a red wizard hat', 'make the armor gold'). Required unless reference_image_base64 is given.

reference_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to copy the appearance of (outfit/colors/details) onto the input image, keeping its pose. Switches the tool into reference mode; description then just refines the instruction. To put an outfit on ANIMATION frames, use transfer_outfit instead.

reference_image_url.description: Alternative to reference_image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the reference PNG. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

width.description: Output width. Defaults to the first input image's width.

height.description: Output height. Defaults to the first input image's height.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the inputs: if any frame has transparency they all stay transparent, otherwise they stay opaque. Pass False to flatten a transparent input onto white.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__edit_image_pixen
tools.description:
Edit an image with a text instruction on the Pixen model (fast, 1 generation).

Returns YOUR image edited — pose, composition and pixel style are preserved
and only what you asked for changes.

Pick between the two edit tools:
- edit_image_pixen — this one; 1 generation, ~10-40s, ONE frame, input max
  256px per side and output max 256x256 in AREA. The default for a single
  sprite.
- edit_image — pro quality, 10-25 generations, ~30-90s, edits up to 16
  frames consistently in one call, accepts a reference image and inputs up
  to 512px. Worth it for animation frames, a character's directions, or when
  pixen's result isn't good enough.

Sizes: the input is capped PER SIDE at 256 (crop an oversized source —
never rescale pixel art); the output is capped by AREA at 256x256 =
65,536px, so 128x512 is fine but 320x320 is not. Output defaults to the
input's size. BOTH sides of both must be multiples of 4 — a 63x222 sprite
is rejected; pad it with transparent pixels to 64x224 first (padding keeps
the pixel grid, rescaling destroys it). Need a bigger canvas? edit_image
takes inputs up to 512.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~10-40 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

tools.description:
Edit one Pro Flash image at its unchanged native canvas size.

Supply image_url (preferred), image_base64, or an owned source_image_id.
method=text requires description; method=reference requires reference_image
({url}, {base64}, or {source_image_id}). References must fit the source canvas.
No-background defaults to the source's transparency. Optional palette
correction matches source colors. Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for exact
shapes. Returns one queued image; poll get_image(job_id), then download.

Cost: by the SOURCE canvas's longest side — 5 generations up to 96px, 6 from
100 to 208, 9 from 212 to 256, for one image. The same ladder as Pro Flash
create and inpaint, and cheaper than edit_image's 10/15/25 tier at every
size. get_pro_flash_capabilities(operation="edit", width=, height=) prices
an exact size for free.

every corner, and shoreline rows between terrains are inserted for you. Name
a terrain the map doesn't have yet and the tileset providing it is attached
automatically, along with any tileset connected to it. A tileset not
connected to this map attaches only when you name its terrain exactly; it
meets the map with hard edges (straight seams) until a tileset joins them.

On a sidescroller map each terrain is a platform top ("grass", "snow") over
its body, and empty cells are air: paint the solid ground. Naming a top the
map lacks attaches the sidescroller tileset that has it.

Cost: free. Painting spends no generations however much you repaint — the
tileset it draws with was paid for when it was generated.

Returns what changed, an ASCII view of the affected area, and — when the edit
used new art or went wrong — a rendered image of it. Pass show=true to see
the image any time; use view_map to look at somewhere you did not just paint.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__edit_map_areas
tools.description:
Declare what blocks movement, as Map Workshop's Gameplay Layers do.

Terrain says what a map LOOKS like; a gameplay layer says what it PLAYS
like. Without one the game falls back to reading the terrain's own names,
so a map is solid or open by accident of vocabulary.

A layer is linked to terrains rather than to an area: the exporter derives
the cells from the terrain grid every time the map is exported, so painting
more water extends the water layer by itself.

    edit_map_areas(map_id, action="add", name="Non-walkable",
                   terrains=["water"], walkable=false)

Call with no action to see the layers a map already has and what the game
makes of each one.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__estimate_skeleton
tools.description:
Estimate the skeleton of a humanoid sprite: its 18 joints, in exactly the
shape animate_with_skeleton_v3 takes.

Two calls: estimate_skeleton(image=...) queues it and returns a job id (usually
done in ~10-20 s, longer when the queue is busy); estimate_skeleton(job_id=...)
returns the keypoints once it is done (wait_for_jobs waits for it).

Pass the result as animate_with_skeleton_v3's `first_frame_keypoints` (the pose
the sprite is in), and use it as the starting point for each frame of
`keypoints` (the motion: move the joints frame by frame). x/y are fractions 0-1
of the image you sent; labels come in the order animate_with_skeleton_v3
lists them.

Humanoids only: the 18 joints are a person's. A fully transparent image is
refused before anything is charged.

Cost: 0.1 generations, charged when the estimate is done.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__expand_object_to_8_directions
tools.description:
Turn one of your 1-direction objects into an 8-direction one, keeping the
same object: its id, tags and animations. Costs 10-25 generations by the
padded canvas (objects up to 168x168; larger ones are refused), ~2-4 min.

The new directions wait for review. get_object shows them (status
review-expansion) and the object stays 1-direction until you decide:
select_object_frames(object_id) with no indices keeps them (the canvas grows
to the review's size, animations move to existing_direction);
dismiss_review(object_id) discards them and leaves the object as it was.

To make a NEW 8-direction object from an image instead, use
create_8_direction_object(reference_image_base64=...).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_character
tools.description:
Get character details, rotation URLs, animations, and download link.
Branches by status: processing (progress+ETA), failed (error+retry), completed (full data).

Download: three ways out, and the last one needs no HTTP at all.
`/mcp/characters/{id}/download` is a ZIP of every completed state in the
group — `?states=` narrows it, taking the state IDS this tool prints on
its `state:` lines, not their names — laid out as
`<state>/rotations/<direction>.png` and
`<state>/animations/<name>/<direction>/frame_000.png` (frame_NNN, 3 digits,
from 000), plus `<state>/portrait.png` and `<state>/vocal/grid.png` where
those exist, and a top-level `metadata.json` giving each state's size,
directions, view, template_id and a `frames` map listing every file — so
the per-direction frame counts are in there as the list lengths. A frame
storage lost shows up as `MISSING_FRAMES.txt` rather than a short ZIP.
`/mcp/characters/{id}/spritesheet` is a ZIP of one sheet PNG + its layout
JSON for THIS state only: row 0 is the rotations, then one row per
animation-direction, uniform cells sized to the largest frame with the rest
transparent padding (nothing is ever resized), and the JSON gives
`cell_size`, `sheet_size`, `columns`, `pivot: "cell-center"` and a row list
naming each row's animation, `animation_group_id`, direction and
frame_count.
To get the pixels back INLINE, with no download and nothing charged:
`pixelart_workbench(argv=["inspect", "character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>"])`
returns that animation's frames as one sheet image in the tool result, with
the canvas and frame durations — `<animation>` is the display name, type or
[group: ...] id this tool prints. `join ref ref --as rows` lays several
animations out one per row (sheets hold at most 1024 px a side).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_lip_sync
tools.description:
Get the lip-sync frame plan for a line of dialogue — for animating in a game.

FREE, and nothing is rendered. Use this instead of create_talking_gif when the
game should animate the mouth itself: you get the spritesheet URL, the row for
the expression, and a frame list giving the column to draw and how long to hold
it. create_talking_gif is the better answer when you just want a playable file.

Timings are exact here — unlike a GIF, an engine can hold a frame for any
duration.

Example:
- get_lip_sync("<uuid>", "Welcome to the village, traveller!")

Returns immediately (no job to poll).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_map
tools.description:
Show a map as an ASCII grid, one character per terrain cell.

With no crop you get the whole map downsampled to fit; pass x/y/width/height
for a 1:1 view of one area. Coordinates are terrain cells and can be
negative — the rulers show the real numbers, so read them off the view and
pass them straight to edit_map.

Maps built from tile groups (isometric, hex, oblique and similar tiles) show
their tile layers: for every cell the tile on top and the stack level it
sits on, plus each stacked column spelled out. Change those with
place_map_tiles.

export="godot" / "unity" / "pixellab" returns a download link for the map
as a game-engine project or the PixelLab ZIP instead of the view.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_object
tools.description:

- processing: progress + ETA
- review: candidate frame URLs + inline previews
- expanding / review-expansion: an 8-direction expansion
  (expand_object_to_8_directions) running, then waiting to be kept or discarded
- completed: rotation URLs, animations, download link
- failed: error + retry hint

metadata.json. A one-direction object with no animations comes back as a
bare PNG instead of a ZIP. `/mcp/objects/{id}/spritesheet` is a ZIP of one

sized to the largest frame (nothing resized), `pivot: "cell-center"`.

`pixelart_workbench(argv=["inspect", "object:<id>:<direction>:<animation>"])`
returns its frames as one sheet image in the tool result. A one-direction
object still needs the direction, and it is the literal `unknown` —
`object:<id>:unknown:<group id>`. `join ref ref --as rows` lays several
animations out one per row (at most 1024 px a side).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_room
tools.description:
A room's state. While it is being made: its stage and progress. When ready: the room
as painted (inline), its download link and its building kit's (a ZIP of the wall, door
and floor tiles it was built from); once its furniture is cut out
(cut_out_room_furniture), its movable pieces by name and the link that opens it in the
website's room editor (move, remove or bring in pieces; shadows follow).

Download: the room as painted is the `download:` PNG. Its cut-out pieces and its
furniture-free floor are in the `layers:` JSON this prints once the pieces are ready
(public, no auth) — you do not need the editor to export them. Keys: `w`/`h` the
room's pixel size; `room` the painting as you see it; `lit` and `unlit` the SAME room
with every piece removed (the empty floor, lit and unlit); `sprites[]` one entry per
piece with `name`, `x`,`y` (its top-left in those pixels), `foot` (the y of its
LOWEST OPAQUE row, where it stands on the floor — not `y` + the PNG's height,
which may end in transparent rows; sort pieces by it to draw them back to front),
`light`, `img` (a transparent PNG as a data URL), `unlit`, and `shadow` {`x`,`y`,`f`}
as its own PNG at its own position, or null where a piece casts none. An isometric room also has `over`: its low front curbs, which go on
top of the pieces. Every image is a `data:image/png;base64,` URL, so decode it rather
than fetching a second file.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__image_to_pixelart
tools.description:
Convert an image, render or photo into pixel art.

This is the general-purpose converter: give it any picture and get pixel art
back at the size you ask for. Use it when a user brings their own artwork,
a screenshot, or an AI render and wants it as a sprite.

Two dials decide how much licence the model takes:
- default (faithful=False, init_image_strength=0) — reinterprets the subject
  as pixel art. Cleanest sprites, least like the original.
- faithful=True with init_image_strength around 100-300 — reproduces the
  source. Use it when the user says "keep it exactly like this". Higher is
  NOT more faithful in a useful way: past ~300 the model stops transforming
  and returns the source image, which is not pixel art.

This is the one converter where YOU pick the output size. When the size does
not matter, image_to_pixelart_pro_flash (6 generations) and
image_to_pixelart_pro (20, tier 1+) redraw more cleanly and pick the size from
the picture.

Related tools: create_portrait_character converts a picture into a character
portrait specifically; unzoom_image is what you want if the input is ALREADY
pixel art that has merely been upscaled — running it through here would
redraw art that only needed downscaling.

Input max area 2048x2048, output max 512x512.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~20-60 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG/JPEG of the image to convert. Any artwork, render or photo. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the source image. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

output_width.description: Width of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source width. Keep the source's aspect ratio.

output_height.description: Height of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source height.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__image_to_pixelart_pro
tools.description:
Convert a picture, render or photo into pixel art with the Pro converter —
the strongest redraw of the three converters.

Which converter:
- image_to_pixelart (1 generation): you choose the exact output width and
  height; faithful mode keeps the source's look. Use it when the size matters.
- image_to_pixelart_pro_flash (6 generations): a clean redraw, output size
  picked from the picture. The default when the size does not matter.
- image_to_pixelart_pro (this, 20 generations, tier 1+): the same automatic
  size, the most careful redraw. Use it when pro_flash's result is not good
  enough.
None of them is for art that is already pixel art but upscaled — that only
needs unzoom_image.

The output size is decided by the conversion (the detected pixel scale) and
reported by get_image. For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8,
any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`:
every pixel of the result is one of them. Transparent areas of the source
become a white background. Sources over 2048px on the longest side are scaled
down first.

Needs a tier 1 subscription or higher.
Cost: 20 generations at any source size. ~1-3 minutes (async). Poll
get_image(job_id).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__inpaint_image
tools.description:
Regenerate one region of an image, keeping everything else pixel-identical.

This is the repair tool: fix a malformed hand, erase a stray pixel cluster,
swap just the cape, add an item to a specific spot. The area outside the
mask is frozen, so the rest of the sprite cannot drift.

Give the area as a rectangle (easiest — you only need coordinates):
  inpaint_image(image_base64=<png>, description="a clean open hand",
                mask_x=18, mask_y=30, mask_width=14, mask_height=14)
or supply your own mask (white = regenerate, black = keep):
  inpaint_image(image_base64=<png>, description="...", mask_image_base64=<png>)

Related: edit_image rewrites the WHOLE image from an instruction (no mask);
create_map_object generates a new object matching a background's style and
returns a transparent cutout, not your edited image.

Image must be 32x32-512x512; above 256px on a side needs a Tier 2 plan.
Cost: 10 generations for any SQUARE canvas up to 256x256 (so 64x64 and 88x88
are both 10), 15 up to 341x341, 25 above. The whole image sets the price, not
the mask. A NON-SQUARE canvas is measured against the nearest of ten aspect
ratios, so BOTH sides count and neither the longest side nor the area decides
it. The 10 ceiling then the 15 ceiling, by ratio: 1:1 256x256 then 341x341 |
5:4 288x232 then 384x309 | 4:3 300x224 then 400x298 | 3:2 316x212 then
421x282 | 16:9 344x192 then 458x256 | 21:9 396x168 then 528x224 (that last
one is past this tool's own 512px side limit, so it is unreachable); a portrait
canvas takes its own ratio's pair swapped (4:5, 3:4, 2:3, 9:16, and anything
taller than 9:16 snaps to 9:16). A canvas fitting inside a ceiling costs that
band and anything past the second one is 25, so 360x168 is 10 and 168x360 is
15, and 220x256 is 10 where 220x400 is 15 and 220x512 is 25.
Generation time: ~30-90 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What should appear in the masked area (e.g. 'a clean four-finger hand holding a sword', 'plain grass, no object').

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to repair. 32x32 to 512x512. Everything outside the mask is preserved exactly. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64, which corrupts the image.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the input: a sprite with transparency stays transparent, an opaque image stays opaque. Pass False to flatten a transparent input onto white.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__inpaint_image_pro_flash
tools.description:
Replace white-mask pixels with Pro Flash, preserving unmasked RGBA bytes exactly.

Source: image_url, image_base64, or owned source_image_id. Mask: a rectangle
(all four mask_x/y/width/height), OR a same-size mask PNG via base64/URL.
Mask RGB must be pure white=generate or black=keep; mask alpha is ignored.
Empty masks are rejected. crop_to_mask is always true. Changes-only output
is transparent outside the mask; Modify current layer returns a composite.
Optional context_image requires bounding_box locating the source and is at
most three times its native dimensions. No images or masks are rescaled.
Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for shapes; poll the job with get_image.

Cost: by the SOURCE canvas's longest side, not the mask — 5 generations up to
96px, 6 from 100 to 208, 9 from 212 to 256, for one image. So a 64x64 repair
is 5 and 128x64 is 6, against inpaint_image's 10 for either. Shrinking the
mask does not lower it. get_pro_flash_capabilities(operation="inpaint",
width=, height=) prices an exact size for free.

schema.name: mcp__pixellab__inpaint_image_pro_flash
schema.description:
Replace white-mask pixels with Pro Flash, preserving unmasked RGBA bytes exactly.

Source: image_url, image_base64, or owned source_image_id. Mask: a rectangle
(all four mask_x/y/width/height), OR a same-size mask PNG via base64/URL.
Mask RGB must be pure white=generate or black=keep; mask alpha is ignored.
Empty masks are rejected. crop_to_mask is always true. Changes-only output
is transparent outside the mask; Modify current layer returns a composite.
Optional context_image requires bounding_box locating the source and is at
most three times its native dimensions. No images or masks are rescaled.
Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for shapes; poll the job with get_image.

Cost: by the SOURCE canvas's longest side, not the mask — 5 generations up to
96px, 6 from 100 to 208, 9 from 212 to 256, for one image. So a 64x64 repair
is 5 and 128x64 is 6, against inpaint_image's 10 for either. Shrinking the
mask does not lower it. get_pro_flash_capabilities(operation="inpaint",
width=, height=) prices an exact size for free.

mask_image_base64.description: Mask PNG, exactly the source size. EVERY pixel's RGB must be pure white (generate) or pure black (keep): a grey or coloured pixel is refused, so remove any antialiasing, and a mask with no white at all is refused too. The mask's own alpha is ignored. Unlike inpaint_image, which does not check this, Pro Flash enforces it. Or give the four mask_x/y/width/height instead.

mask_image_url.description: Same mask as mask_image_base64, from an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL.

context_image.description: The surrounding scene to match, not a style reference. Pass it WITH bounding_box or not at all. At most 3x the source canvas in each dimension and never rescaled. Exactly ONE of its three sources.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

bounding_box.description: Where the source canvas sits inside context_image: width/height must equal the source size, and the box must lie entirely within the context image.

no_background.description: Background removal on the GENERATED pixels. Left out it follows the source: on if the source has any non-opaque pixel, off if it is fully opaque. Removal runs before the frozen pixels are copied back, so masked pixels CAN come back transparent (how a bigger hairstyle keeps gaps around it) and pixels outside the mask are untouched either way. Off, the render is drawn on a background, so the masked area comes back opaque.

output_method.description: What comes back, always at the source's own size. `Modify current layer` (default) is the whole sprite with the mask area replaced. `Modify current layer, only changes` and `New layer with changes` are that same canvas holding ONLY the masked pixels, fully transparent everywhere else - a layer to drop over your own art. Every pixel outside the mask is copied from your source byte for byte, and that copy is the LAST step, after background removal and palette work, so nothing outside the mask can shift.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__inpaint_map
tools.description:
Regenerate one rectangular area of a map with AI — a ramp, a broken wall, a
path through a forest, a seam between two terrains — the way Map Workshop's
inpainting does. Give the area in the same cells get_map and edit_map use.

Choosing the area: put what you want near its centre and make it a bit
larger than that, with a cell or two of the map you keep on every side. The
model blends the new pixels into what it sees at the area's edges; something
that runs into an edge (a stream, a wall) can end in a visible step where the
area stops.

The new pixels go into the map's inpainted layer, which sits over the
terrain and under objects, exactly where Map Workshop puts its own
inpainting; the terrain cells underneath are unchanged.

Cost: like inpaint_image_pro_flash, by the area's longest side in pixels — 5
generations up to 96px, 6 up to 208px, 9 up to 256px. Not available on
sidescroller maps or maps with tile layers (the area could not be drawn here
as Map Workshop shows it).

Non-blocking: returns a job_id. Poll inpaint_map(map_id=..., job_id=...);
when the job completes the result is written into the map (also
automatically) and the poll shows the area.

Make one of your songs into game music that loops seamlessly.

The song is made again so that the part between its intro and its ending
repeats without a seam: two new takes, each with loop points. Play the take to

intro plays once, the ending never. Instrumental songs only, for now.

Cost: 4 generations, or $0.033 in credits; charged once the takes are made.
Needs a tier 2 subscription or higher.

Generation time: ~1.5-2.5 minutes (async). Poll with get_music or wait_for_jobs.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__pixelart_workbench
tools.description:
Run one pixel-art command on a drawing or image you already made. This is
the engine's own command line: it checks work, explains it and improves it.

Commands: check and explain (read-only):
- lint <id> [--rules outline_gap,orphan_pixel,...] — pixel-art defects, each
  naming the node and command that drew them
- inspect <id> --region x0,y0,x1,y1 --scale 10 — a zoomed crop with its
  exact colours, to LOOK at: the id it returns still holds the whole
  picture, so passing it on sends the full canvas and not the region.
  `split ... --count` below is what actually cuts a piece out
- measure <id> --at x,y — what is at a pixel and who drew it
- explain <id> — resolved geometry, per-command footprints, before rendering
- motion / storyboard / silhouette / reveal / clusters / parts <id> — reports
- score <id> — a 0-100 pixel-art discipline score with a breakdown
- compare <id> <id> — two results side by side
Improve (returns a NEW drawing id):
- shade <id> --band 2 --light=-1,-1 — banded shading along a colour ramp
- selout <id> — selective outlining; reoutline / clean-lines / aa / mirror
- cluster <id> --at x,y --action recolor --color <name> — one guarded cluster
- repair <id> — deterministic cleanup of drift, strays, fringe and noise
Sheets and frames (returns a NEW image id):
- split <image> --grid 3x3 [--count n] — a sprite sheet, strip or grid as an
  animation, one frame per cell (columns x rows). --count keeps the first n
  cells and drops the rest, so `split <image> --grid 2x1 --count 1` is the
  free exact crop of the left half, `--grid 1x2 --count 1` the top half, and
  a one-cell result downloads as image.png (a multi-frame one has no
  image.png, only frames.png — which is why a plain 2x1 split cannot be
  handed on as a single picture). Cells must divide the canvas evenly; the
  error names the counts that fit. Without --count, trailing cells that are
  one flat colour are dropped
- join <image> <image> ... [--as sheet|rows|animation] [--columns n] — pictures
  or animations as one sprite sheet, one per row, or one animation
- scale <image> --by 4 — the same picture or animation bigger, each pixel a
  4x4 block (a sticker, a print); nothing is redrawn
A result comes back as an image in the reply AND as a no-auth URL the reply
prints, `/mcp/pixel-tools/<id>/image.png` (`frames.png` for the frames of a
multi-frame one) — so a sheet you joined is both readable inline and
downloadable. Sheets hold at most 1024 px a side; `join` refuses a larger
one rather than shrinking the art, and says how many frames do fit.
Craft operations need colour ramps: run `extract-palette <id>` first, then
pass `--ramps skin=dark,mid,light`.
Authoring: `edit <id> --changes '[...]'` applies exact pixel operations and
`draw <id> --recipe '{...}'` builds or revises a layered scene; both take JSON
whose fields are NOT listed here. Colours in that JSON are always `#RRGGBB`
or `#RRGGBBAA` with alpha `00` or `ff` — `rgb()` and bare hex are refused,
and nothing strips the `#`, since argv is a JSON list rather than a shell
line. Every `edit` change carries `operation`, `layer`, `frames` (ONE-based)
and `reason`; coordinates are zero-based and a `region` is `[x0,y0,x1,y1]`
inclusive. Then its own fields: `patch_pixels` takes `pixels`, a list of
`[x,y,expected,replacement]` (1-10000, each assigned only where the pixel
already holds `expected`, so a mismatch fails the pass); `copy_region` takes
`source_layer`, `source_frame`, `region`, `at` `[x,y]`; `map_colors` takes
`region` and `colors` `{"#from":"#to"}` (alpha must match); `flood_fill`
`seed`/`expected`/`color`; `brush` `points` plus `color`; `outline` `mode`
(outside|inside|recolor|erase). The full contracts and any command's flags
are one free call away: `describe edits | paint | outline | draw | animation
| motion | scenes | review`, `<command> -h`, `describe cli`.
Free for subscribers.

prints, `/mcp/pixel-tools/<id>/image.png` (`frames.png` for the frames of a
multi-frame one) — so a sheet you joined is both readable inline and
downloadable. Sheets hold at most 1024 px a side; `join` refuses a larger
one rather than shrinking the art, and says how many frames do fit.
Craft operations need colour ramps: run `extract-palette <id>` first, then
pass `--ramps skin=dark,mid,light`.
Authoring: `edit <id> --changes '[...]'` applies exact pixel operations and
`draw <id> --recipe '{...}'` builds or revises a layered scene; both take JSON
whose fields are NOT listed here. Colours in that JSON are always `#RRGGBB`
or `#RRGGBBAA` with alpha `00` or `ff` — `rgb()` and bare hex are refused,
and nothing strips the `#`, since argv is a JSON list rather than a shell
line. Every `edit` change carries `operation`, `layer`, `frames` (ONE-based)
and `reason`; coordinates are zero-based and a `region` is `[x0,y0,x1,y1]`
inclusive. Then its own fields: `patch_pixels` takes `pixels`, a list of
`[x,y,expected,replacement]` (1-10000, each assigned only where the pixel
already holds `expected`, so a mismatch fails the pass); `copy_region` takes
`source_layer`, `source_frame`, `region`, `at` `[x,y]`; `map_colors` takes
`region` and `colors` `{"#from":"#to"}` (alpha must match); `flood_fill`
`seed`/`expected`/`color`; `brush` `points` plus `color`; `outline` `mode`
(outside|inside|recolor|erase). The full contracts and any command's flags
are one free call away: `describe edits | paint | outline | draw | animation
| motion | scenes | review`, `<command> -h`, `describe cli`.
Free for subscribers.

argv.description: One command line, e.g. 'lint <drawing_id> --rules outline_gap' or ['edit', '<id>', '--changes', '[...]']. Omit it for the playbook. A subject is an id or an image reference — never a file path; the server writes the output and returns a new id. A reference is `character:<id>:<direction>` for a rotation, `character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>` for every frame of that animation (the display name, type or [group: ...] id get_character prints), the same two forms for `object:<id>` (a one-direction object's direction is the literal `unknown`), `gallery:<id>`, `job:<id>`, `upload:<id>`, a data URL, an https link or base64. That is how a stored animation's pixels come back inline without downloading anything. Start with 'describe cli' for the full command list.

mode.description: low (default): act directly, fewest tokens — one decisive image per result. high: think openly — fuller evidence and a review checklist; write your plan and observations in `notes`. Use the mode the user asked for.

notes.description: What you observed and what this step should achieve, in a few sentences (high mode: always; low: optional). On the first call, include the user's request. Stored with the step to improve these tools.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__place_map_object
tools.description:
Place objects or characters on a map, at a terrain cell or an exact pixel.

Objects are how a map gets trees, houses, rocks and NPCs — terrain painting
(edit_map) only covers ground. A tileset tiles a SURFACE, so anything with a
silhouette has to be an object.

Position: x/y stands the sprite on that cell (the coordinates get_map
shows). world_x/world_y puts it at an exact world pixel instead, as Map
Workshop's free drag does — use it to match positions from a game scene or
an isometric layout that does not fall on the cell grid.

For many objects pass `placements`: one call, one save.

Returns a picture of the result by default, because a placement that is one
cell off, or far bigger than you expected, is invisible in text.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__place_map_tiles
tools.description:
Place, stack and erase tiles on a map's tile layers — the map editor's tile
painting, with its Stack layer control.

A map made from tile groups (isometric, hex, oblique, square tiles) keeps
each group as a tile layer; get_map lists them and shows, per cell, the
tile on top and its stack level. A cell holds a column of tiles: level 0
is the ground, and each level above sits one tile height higher, so a
`stack` of 3 builds a pillar and "on_top" builds on whatever is there.

Placing on a cell's level replaces the tile already there. As in the
editor, a tile placed on one ground layer clears that same cell and level
on any other ground layer drawn on the same grid.

Tiles go down exactly as given: for connected sets, pick the tile drawn
for that spot's neighbours (get_tiles_pro lists each tile's mask).

A building kit is several layers: floor, interior walls, outer walls, roof
(when the kit has roof pieces) and pieces (pillars, doorways, stairs). Lay
floor tiles and the outer walls follow the floor's outline. Interior walls
and roofs take no tile: each cell's piece follows its neighbours. A doorway
is cut into the wall at that cell, and stairs lay both halves. get_map lists
what each kit layer takes.

Returns what changed and a view of the area: the top tile and the top
level of every cell, and each stacked column level by level.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__reduce_colors
tools.description:
Quantize images onto a smaller, shared palette.

Pixel art reads as pixel art partly because of its restricted palette. AI
output and converted artwork often carry hundreds of near-identical colors;
this snaps them onto a tight palette, optionally with ordered dithering.

Passing several frames in one call is the point: they are quantized TOGETHER,
so an animation or a character's eight directions come back sharing ONE
palette instead of drifting apart frame by frame. Quantizing them one at a
time is the mistake this tool exists to prevent.

Three ways to choose the palette:
- omit num_colors and the palette image — the size is auto-detected
- num_colors — quantize to exactly this many colors
- palette_image — reuse the colors of an existing image (the game's palette)

The result carries a `palette` strip you can feed back as palette_image_base64
to lock later frames onto the same colors.

Total size limit across all frames is 512x512 worth of pixels (sixteen 64x64
frames, or four 128x128).

Cost: 0.1 generations. Runs locally in about a second — poll once with
get_image(job_id).

transparency. Same size in and out.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__remove_from_project
tools.description:
Stop a game project from using a character, object, tileset, map, room, UI
asset, song or sound effect, or take an asset out of a folder (or a tile group
or isometric tile out of the game it is filed under).

This unlinks the art from the project. It does NOT delete the art: the
asset stays in your library and can be added back at any time, and any
other project using it is untouched. Use delete_character / delete_object /
delete_topdown_tileset / delete_map / delete_room to actually destroy something.

Until now add_to_project had no inverse, so a project could accumulate art
it no longer used — and a map that fails to export blocks every deploy of
that project, with no way back out.

The kind is worked out from the id; you do not have to say which it is.
Calling twice is harmless.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__save_to_asset
tools.description:
Save pixel art into one of your characters, objects, Creator gallery
images or tilesets, replacing a rotation, one direction of an animation, a
gallery image or a tileset's tiles — or add it to the gallery as a new image
(free, no generation).

Use it to keep a fix made with pixelart_workbench or another image tool: the
character and object creators, the Creator gallery, the map editor, downloads
and game projects then show the new pixels. The image must match what it replaces —
the same canvas size and the same number of frames; a different size can go
to the gallery as a new image. Save each direction with its own call. The
replaced frames are kept: the reply gives the save_to_asset call that puts
them back.

Examples:
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:south")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:east:<group id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="object:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:new",
  description="knight holding a sword, idle")
- save_to_asset(image="<edited sheet>", target="tileset:<id>")

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__select_object_frames

Promote selected frames of a review object to individual completed objects.

See get_object on a review-status object to view candidates inline.
Each selected index becomes its own 1-direction object. Once no frames
remain in the review object it is deleted automatically. If a call times

leave the review object, and re-selecting one is refused).

On an 8-direction expansion review (expand_object_to_8_directions, status
review-expansion), call it with no indices to keep the expansion: the same
object becomes 8-direction, its canvas grows to the review's size and its
animations move to the expansion's existing direction.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__set_canvas_size
tools.description:
Change a character's or object's canvas size by adding or removing transparent margin. Free.

Every rotation is re-centred on the new canvas about its pivot. The art is
never scaled or cropped: a size smaller than the art itself is refused with
the art's bounds. Animations keep the canvas they were made on; an object's
map placements follow it. Use it to give a sprite room before animating
(a sword swing, a jump) or to trim empty margin.

talking expressions (no generation, free).

A portrait is the starting frame for talking animations — set one, then
create_vocal_animation generates the mouth positions from it. Overwrites any
existing portrait. Pass exactly one of image, from_job_id, remove_portrait or

- Straight from a portrait job:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", from_job_id="<portrait-job-uuid>")
- From your own artwork:

- Delete the portrait:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", remove_portrait=True)
- Delete the angry expression, keep the rest:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", remove_expression="angry")
